-   \(i\) **volumes** (voxelize into a 3D grid — 3D convolutions possible but cubic cost; sparse trees/octrees for the worst case);
-   \(ii\) **raw points** (PointNet: MLP per point + global max = symmetric function, permutation invariance; its successors add a local neighborhood);
-   \(iii\) **range images** (*range images*: project the cloud onto a spherical image whose every pixel encodes the distance — 2D CNNs then apply as-is, see LU-Net in ch. 11).

The choice is a memory/precision/speed trade-off — over $10^9$ points, family (iii) is unbeatable and feeds the real-time systems of autonomous vehicles.
:::

## 11. Research at IGN (Brédif): urban LiDAR {#ch11}

The module is taught by Mathieu Brédif, researcher at IGN (MATIS laboratory, ENSG) and professor at Université Gustave Eiffel. His work traverses exactly the program of the semester: mobile acquisition, registration, semantic analysis of urban clouds, and the handling of LiDAR sampling defects. Verified selection:

-   **TerraMobilita/iQmulus urban benchmark.** B. Vallet, M. Brédif, A. Serna, B. Marcotegui, N. Paparoditis, "[TerraMobilita/iQmulus urban point cloud analysis benchmark](https://hal.science/hal-01167995)", *Computers & Graphics* 49, 2015 — an annotated dataset acquired by *Stéréopolis* (IGN's mobile mapping vehicle) in Paris and Rueil-Malmaison, with two evaluation tasks: facade segmentation and urban object classification (see [data.ign.fr](https://data.ign.fr/benchmarks/UrbanAnalysis/)). The international reference for comparing mobile cloud analysis methods — the "test bench" of ch. 8-10.
-   **Semantic segmentation by range images: LU-Net.** P. Biasutti, V. Lepetit, M. Brédif, J.-F. Aujol, A. Bugeau, "[LU-Net: An Efficient Network for 3D LiDAR Point Cloud Semantic Segmentation Based on End-to-End-Learned 3D Features and U-Net](https://hal.science/hal-02269915)", ICCV Workshops 2019 — the architecture of ch. 9 (U-Net) applied to the range images of ch. 10, with 3D features learned end to end: the "signs, lampposts, facades" class at a fraction of the cost of 3D convolutions.
-   **LiDAR disocclusion and visibility.** Mobile LiDARs see streets *from the street*: everything occluded (behind a car, a tree) is missing from the cloud.

    The series of works "[Disocclusion of 3D LiDAR point clouds using range images](https://hal.science/hal-01522366)" (ISPRS Hannover Workshop 2017), "Visibility estimation in point clouds with variable density" (VISAPP 2019), and "Diffusion and inpainting of reflectance and height LiDAR orthoimages" (*Computer Vision and Image Understanding* 179, 2019), with P. Biasutti, J.-F. Aujol, A. Bugeau — extended as early as ICIP 2016 with M. Bevilacqua ("Visibility estimation and joint inpainting of Lidar depth maps") —, addresses these holes: estimating visibility, inpainting range and ortho-reflectance images — LiDAR processed as an image (ch. 2), with geometry as a constraint.
-   **3D models and historical textures.** His recent work projects very many photographs (heritage ones included) onto current urban 3D models — projective "multitexturing" of cities and clouds (with M. S. Gomes de Castro) — an exercise in homographies (ch. 5) and visibility (ch. 10) at the scale of a city. See his [full CV on HAL](https://cv.hal.science/mathieu-bredif).

::: note
[Note — The guiding thread]{.tag} One theme connects this work: *processing massive 3D data with well-tuned 2D tools* — range images, U-Net, inpainting — while respecting the geometry of the sensor. This is exactly the approach of ch. 1 to 10: model the formation (ch. 1), choose the representation (ch. 10), then apply the right machinery (ch. 9). The module's project topics draw on the TerraMobilita benchmark and IGN's open data.
:::

## Exercises {#ex}

1.  **★ Camera (solved).** Sensor 3000×2000 of 2.2 µm, focal length 24 mm. (a) Horizontal field of view? (b) Focal length in pixels? (c) How many point pairs for a homography, and why 4? (d) Does a pure rotation of the camera give a homography between views (justify)? *Solution.* (a) $w = 6.6$ mm, $\mathrm{FOV} = 2\arctan(3.3/24) \approx 15.6^\circ$. (b) $f_x = 0.024/2.2\,\text{µm} \approx 10\,900$ px. (c) 4 pairs: $H$ has 8 dof (9 coefficients − 1 scale), each pair provides 2 independent equations (Prop. 5.3). (d) Yes: Theorem 5.2, case (ii) — it is even the only non-planar case that qualifies.
2.  **★ Convolution (solved).** (a) Convolve $[10, 12, 11, 40, 42]$ with the kernel $[0.25,\,0.5,\,0.25]$ (replicated borders). (b) How many multiplications per pixel for a 5×5 Gaussian, direct then separable? (c) Why is a 3×3 box filter *not* an ideal smoother? *Solution.* (a) $[10.5,\,11.25,\,18.5,\,33.25,\,41.5]$ — the jump 11→40 is smoothed over two samples. (b) 25 direct, $2\times5 = 10$ separated (Prop. 2.2), ratio 2.5×. (c) its frequency response is a sinc (Def. 2.1 and the *Signal Processing* module, ch. 3): negative lobes create contrast reversals at high frequencies — the Gaussian has no rebound.
3.  **★ Lucas-Kanade (solved).** Window of 4 pixels, measurements $(I_x, I_y\,;\,I_t)$: (2, 1; 6), (4, 2; 10), (3, 1; 7), (5, 2; 12). Solve for the flow; compute the eigenvalues of the tensor; is the flow reliable? Propose two remedies.

    *Solution.* $M = \begin{pmatrix}54 & 23\\ 23 & 10\end{pmatrix}$, right-hand side $-(133, 57)^\top$. $\det M = 11$ — nearly singular: $\lambda_1 \approx 63.8$, $\lambda_2 \approx 0.17$. Cramer: $u = v = -19/11 \approx -1.73$.

    Reliability: no — $\lambda_2 \ll \lambda_1$ signals an edge (aperture problem, Thm 7.2); the uncertainty ellipse is very elongated: the flow component along the edge is poorly observed. Remedies: pyramid (large → small motion) and Gaussian weighting of the window; failing that, reject the pixel ($\lambda_2 < \tau$).
4.  **★ Stereo (solved).** $f = 721$ px, $B = 0.54$ m. (a) Disparity of an object at 25 m, at 5 m? (b) Depth if $d = 25$ px? (c) Depth uncertainty at 25 m if the disparity is known to ±0.25 px? (d) Why double the baseline?

    *Solution.* (a) $d = fB/Z$: 15.6 px at 25 m; 77.9 px at 5 m. (b) $Z = fB/d = 721\times0.54/25 \approx 15.6$ m. (c) $\Delta Z/Z = \Delta d/d = 0.25/15.6 \approx 1.6\,\%$ → ±0.4 m (Thm 6.3). (d) $Z = fB/d$: doubling $B$ doubles $d$ at equal depth, hence *halves* the relative error — at the price of a wider separation and increased occlusion areas between views.
5.  **★★ Harris in practice.** Implement the structure tensor (Example 4.6), threshold $R > 0.01\,R_{max}$, display the corners on a photo; compare with `cv2.cornerMinEigenVal`. Rotate the image by 30° and measure the stability of the detection (Prop. 4.3). *Hint:* smoothing with $\sigma \approx 1{-}2$ before the Sobels; measure stability by the number of corners rematched within ±2 px.
6.  **★★ RANSAC.** (a) Derive the formula for the number of draws $N \geq \ln(1-p)/\ln(1-w^s)$ for an $s$-point estimator (independence of the draws).

    \(b\) Compute $N$ for $s = 4$, $w = 0.3$, $p = 0.999$. (c) Adaptive RANSAC: how to stop before $N$ draws?

    *Hint:* (a) failure probability $1-w^s$ per draw, independent ⇒ $(1-w^s)^N \leq 1-p$. (b) $w^4 = 0.0081$, $N = 6.908/0.00813 \approx 850$. (c) update $w$ with the current best consensus and recompute $N$ on the fly.
7.  **★★ ICP.** Generate a noisy planar cloud, transform it (30° rotation), run the ICP of Example 10.5 from increasingly bad initializations; measure the basin of convergence. Test the point-to-plane variant on planes. *Hint:* plot the RMS error per iteration (log); the basin closes when matches cross the edges of the cloud — hence the value of rejecting distant pairs and of initial RANSAC.
8.  **★★ Segmentation, up close.** On a photo, compare k-means on (a) RGB, (b) RGB + $(x, y)/10$, (c) Lab; choose $k$ by the elbow method. Where do SLIC superpixels fit in a modern vision pipeline (ch. 8-9)? *Hint:* (b) forces spatial compactness — connected regions; (c) separates hue from luminance (Def. 1.5); connect to the *Machine Learning* module, ch. 7.
9.  **★★ Graph cut by hand (solved).** Three pixels in a row, a – b – c. As in Example 8.5, the edge from $s$ to a pixel carries the cost of the background label, and the edge to $t$ the cost of the foreground label: 6 and 1 for pixel a, 3 and 2 for b, 1 and 5 for c. Both neighbour edges have $\lambda B = 2$.

    \(a\) Find a maximum flow by augmenting paths, and the minimum cut (Algorithm 8.4). (b) Check the result by listing the energies of Definition 8.3. (c) From which value of $\lambda B$ does the whole row become foreground?

    *Solution.* (a) The paths $s \to a \to t$, $s \to b \to t$ and $s \to c \to t$ carry 1, 2 and 1; then $s \to a \to b \to c \to t$ carries 2: the flow is 6.

    Then $S = \{s, a, b\}$: pixels a and b are foreground, c is background, and the cut $1 + 1 + 2 + 2 = 6$ equals the flow.

    \(b\) The labelling (F, F, B) costs $1 + 2 + 1 + 2 = 6$; (F, B, B) costs 7, (F, F, F) 8, (B, B, B) 10, and the four others more. (c) (F, F, F) costs 8 and (F, F, B) costs $4 + \lambda B$: the whole row is foreground once $\lambda B > 4$.

## Projects and assessment {#projects}

The official assessment is "5 small classes (TD) + 1 project", stated in the description of the 2026–2027 SynapseS sheet and in its section for the engineering degree; the LLGA section of the sheet displays no assessment of its own. The subjects below are proposals of these notes, not official rules. The exercises and the labs of the session plan match the five small classes, and one solo or group subject stands for the project; the sheet announces no written exam, so the exam below is only a proposal, for instance for a resit.

The projects exercise mainly O6 (vision, the visual side of the multimodal objective), O7 (complete pipelines on real benchmarks, checked against OpenCV, COLMAP or torchvision) and O1 (SVD, least squares and CNN training), with O4 and O5 in the graph-cut, LiDAR-graph and scene-graph subjects.

### Solo projects {#projects-solo}

1.  **[Solo · ≈ 20 h] Panorama stitcher from scratch.** When does a handheld panorama break the homography model of Theorem 5.2, and how many RANSAC draws does matching really need?
    -   *Work*: Harris and SIFT matching with Lowe's ratio test, Hartley-normalized DLT, adaptive RANSAC whose number of draws is measured against Proposition 5.4, inverse warping with bilinear interpolation, and feathered blending; the method of Brown and Lowe ("Automatic Panoramic Image Stitching using Invariant Features", IJCV 2007).
    -   *Data*: the 59 viewpoint sequences of HPatches (Balntas, Lenc, Vedaldi and Mikolajczyk, CVPR 2017), which come with ground-truth homographies; then your own sequences, on a tripod (pure rotation), of a planar facade, and handheld with parallax — the two cases of Theorem 5.2 and one failure.
    -   *Success criterion*: mean corner error of the estimated homographies under 3 px on most HPatches viewpoint pairs; measured draws compared with Proposition 5.4; seams and ghosting compared with `cv2.Stitcher` and explained.
    -   *Deliverables*: code, a 4–6 page report, a 10-minute talk; chapters 2, 4 and 5.
2.  **[Solo · ≈ 20 h] Paper study: how robust is ICP, and does optimal transport help? (Besl and McKay, 1992; Shen, Feydy et al., NeurIPS 2021).** How wide is the basin of convergence of point-to-point, point-to-plane and trimmed ICP, and does a soft transport matching widen it?
    -   *Work*: starting from Example 10.5, map the success rate against the initial rotation, the noise, the overlap and density changes; add an entropic-OT (Sinkhorn) soft matching computed with the POT library, as in the RobOT paper, and a RANSAC initialization on Open3D's FPFH features.
    -   *Data*: the Stanford Bunny scans `bun000` and `bun045` of the Stanford 3D Scanning Repository (partial overlap), and the synthetic clouds of Example 10.5.
    -   *Success criterion*: success-rate curves (final rotation error under 2°) against the initial angle for each method, with the RMS per iteration and the time per run; the OT variant compared at equal time budget.
    -   *Deliverables*: code, report, talk; chapters 0 and 10. It leads to [Computational Optimal Transport, ch. 3](../m1p2-optimal-transport/index.html#ch3) (Sinkhorn) and to the ICP of [Shapes, ch. 4](../m1p1-shapes/index.html#ch4).
3.  **[Solo · ≈ 20 h] Graph cuts against learned segmentation.** With the same user input, how close does an interactive graph cut get to a pretrained promptable segmenter?
    -   *Work*: Boykov-Jolly segmentation (Definition 8.3) with Gaussian $B_{pq}$ and colour-histogram terminal costs, solved with the PyMaxflow library (Boykov-Kolmogorov); a sweep of the Potts weight $\lambda$; k-means and SLIC baselines; a normalized cut of the same pixel graph on downsampled images; Segment Anything (Kirillov et al., ICCV 2023) prompted with the same box.
    -   *Data*: the GrabCut dataset (Rother, Kolmogorov and Blake, SIGGRAPH 2004): 50 images with ground-truth masks and the user trimaps of the paper.
    -   *Success criterion*: mean IoU over the 50 images for each method with identical user input; the effect of $\lambda$ explained with Example 8.5.
    -   *Deliverables*: code, report, talk; chapters 8 and 9. The normalized cut is the spectral clustering of [Graph ML, ch. 4](../m1p2-graph-ml/index.html#ch4).

### Group projects {#projects-group}

1.  **[Group of 3 · ≈ 30 h each] From two views to multi-view stereo and novel views.** How close can a pipeline written from the chapters get to COLMAP, and where does it break?
    -   *Work*: calibrate a phone camera (Zhang's checkerboard, ch. 1); normalized 8-point algorithm with RANSAC, decomposition of $E$ and the chirality test (Proposition 6.2); triangulation and incremental SfM with bundle adjustment by `scipy.optimize.least_squares` (Definition 6.5); plane-sweep NCC on 5–10 views (Definition 6.8); interpolated views (Example 6.10) and, as a stretch, a 3D Gaussian splatting fit from the recovered poses.
    -   *Data*: your own captures, then one scene of the ETH3D high-resolution multi-view benchmark (Schöps et al., CVPR 2017), which provides laser-scan ground truth.
    -   *Split*: calibration and two-view geometry; SfM and bundle adjustment; multi-view stereo and rendering.
    -   *Success criterion*: camera rotations within 2° of COLMAP's; accuracy and completeness of the fused cloud against the ETH3D scan at a 5 cm tolerance; disocclusion holes shown and explained.
    -   *Deliverables*: code, an 8–10 page joint report, a 20-minute talk; chapters 1, 5 and 6.
2.  **[Group of 3 · ≈ 30 h each] Urban LiDAR segmentation: range image, points or graph?** Which representation of Proposition 10.6 gives the best accuracy per unit of memory and time on street scans?
    -   *Work*: three pipelines under the same budget — (i) a range image and a U-Net in the style of LU-Net (ch. 11); (ii) PointNet on raw points; (iii) a GNN over the $k$-nearest-neighbour graph, with PCA normals as node features (Proposition 10.2).
    -   *Data*: a subset of SemanticKITTI (Behley et al., ICCV 2019), two training sequences and the validation sequence 08; as a stretch, the TerraMobilita/iQmulus benchmark (Vallet et al., 2015) of ch. 11.
    -   *Split*: one pipeline per member, with shared data loading and evaluation.
    -   *Success criterion*: mIoU on the held-out sequence, memory and latency per scan for the three pipelines; an analysis of the errors in occluded areas (ch. 11).
    -   *Deliverables*: code, joint report, talk; chapters 9–11. Pipeline (iii) is the message passing of [Graph ML, ch. 5](../m1p2-graph-ml/index.html#ch5).
3.  **[Group of 3 · ≈ 30 h each] Scene graphs from detections, the perception front end of Y1.5.** How much does detection error degrade the scene graph, and the answers computed on it?
    -   *Work*: fine-tune a detector with attribute heads (colour, shape, material, size) as in the lab sheet of ch. 9; build the scene graph of the Note in ch. 9, with *left of* and *behind* from the box positions; answer a few CLEVR question families with a symbolic program executor, on gold and on predicted graphs.
    -   *Data*: CLEVR (Johnson et al., CVPR 2017), about 10,000 training and 2,000 validation renders, with full scene annotations and question programs.
    -   *Split*: detector and attributes; scene-graph builder and its metrics; question executor and evaluation.
    -   *Success criterion*: AP@0.5 per attribute class; edge precision and recall of the predicted scene graphs against the annotations; question accuracy on gold against predicted graphs, as a function of the detection threshold.
    -   *Deliverables*: code, joint report, talk; chapters 1, 5 and 9. It is the first milestone of the Year 1 project [Y1.5](../../projects/index.html#y1-5) and feeds the relational GNNs of [Graph ML, ch. 5](../m1p2-graph-ml/index.html#ch5).

### Written exam (proposal) {#projects-exam}

Two hours, one handwritten A4 sheet allowed, a simple calculator allowed; four exercises.

1.  **Question (5 points).** Explain why the Harris response is invariant to a rotation of the image but not to a change of scale. List the steps by which SIFT obtains scale and rotation invariance, then state Lowe's edge-rejection test and say what it rejects.
    -   *Expected*: $M$ averages $\nabla I\,\nabla I^\top$, and a rotation maps it to $RMR^\top$: same eigenvalues, same response (Proposition 4.3). A zoom changes which pixels fall in the window, so a corner at one scale looks like an edge or a flat area at another.
    -   SIFT: extrema of the DoG in $(x, y, \sigma)$ for scale; the dominant gradient orientation for rotation; a $4\times4\times8$ histogram, normalized and clipped at 0.2, for illumination.
    -   Edge test: keep a point only if $\det H > 0$ and $\mathrm{tr}(H)^2/\det H < (r+1)^2/r$, with $r = 10$; it rejects edge-like points, whose principal curvatures differ by a factor above 10.
2.  **Question (5 points).** A rectified stereo rig has $f = 700$ px and $B = 0.5$ m. (a) Give the depth of a point with disparity 14 px, and its uncertainty if the disparity is known to ±0.5 px. (b) $F$ is estimated by RANSAC on 8-point samples with 50% inliers: how many draws give 99% confidence? And with the 7-point algorithm?
    -   *Expected*: $Z = fB/d = 350/14 = 25$ m, and $\Delta Z \approx Z^2\Delta d/(fB) \approx 0.89$ m, that is 3.6% (Example 6.4).
    -   By Proposition 5.4,
        $$
        N \geq \frac{\ln(0.01)}{\ln(1 - 0.5^8)} = \frac{4.605}{0.00391} \approx 1177
        $$
        draws; with 7 points, $4.605/0.00784 \approx 588$: one point fewer per sample halves the number of draws at this inlier rate.
3.  **Question (5 points).** Let $p_i, q_i$ ($i = 1, \dots, n$) be paired points of $\mathbb{R}^3$, with centred versions $\tilde p_i = p_i - \bar p$ and $\tilde q_i = q_i - \bar q$, and consider
    $$
    \min_{R \in SO(3),\ t \in \mathbb{R}^3} \ \sum_i \|R p_i + t - q_i\|^2, \qquad H = \sum_i \tilde p_i \tilde q_i^\top = U\Lambda V^\top .
    $$
    Prove that the optimal translation is $t = \bar q - R\bar p$, that the best rotation then maximizes $\mathrm{tr}(RH)$, and that it is $R = VU^\top$ when $\det(VU^\top) = 1$.
    -   *Expected*: the gradient in $t$, $2\sum_i (R p_i + t - q_i)$, vanishes at $t = \bar q - R\bar p$.
    -   Substituting, the cost becomes
        $$
        \sum_i\|\tilde p_i\|^2 + \sum_i\|\tilde q_i\|^2 - 2\sum_i \tilde q_i^\top R\,\tilde p_i , \qquad \sum_i \tilde q_i^\top R\,\tilde p_i = \mathrm{tr}(RH) .
        $$
    -   With $Z = V^\top R U$, which is orthogonal,
        $$
        \mathrm{tr}(RU\Lambda V^\top) = \mathrm{tr}(Z\Lambda) = \sum_i Z_{ii}\lambda_i \leq \sum_i \lambda_i ,
        $$
        since $Z_{ii} \leq 1$ and $\lambda_i \geq 0$. Equality holds at $Z = I$, that is $R = VU^\top$, a rotation since its determinant is 1 (Theorem 10.3).
4.  **Question (5 points).** One class, boxes written $(x_1, y_1, x_2, y_2)$. Two ground truths and four detections, sorted by decreasing score:
    $$
    G_1 = (0, 0, 4, 4),\ G_2 = (10, 0, 14, 4); \qquad D_1 = (0, 0, 4, 4),\ D_2 = (1, 0, 5, 4),\ D_3 = (10, 2, 14, 6),\ D_4 = (11, 0, 15, 4).
    $$
    (a) Compute the IoU of $D_2$ with $G_1$ and of $D_3$, $D_4$ with $G_2$. (b) Which detections survive NMS at 0.5? (c) Give the AP at $\tau = 0.5$, without and with NMS.
    -   *Expected*: (a) $12/20 = 0.6$; $8/24 \approx 0.33$; $12/20 = 0.6$.
    -   \(b\) $\mathrm{IoU}(D_1, D_2) = 0.6 > 0.5$ removes $D_2$; $\mathrm{IoU}(D_3, D_4) = 6/26 \approx 0.23$ keeps both. $D_1$, $D_3$ and $D_4$ survive.
    -   \(c\) Without NMS the verdicts are TP, FP (duplicate), FP, TP: precision 1 up to recall 0.5, then 0.5 at recall 1, so $\mathrm{AP} = 0.5 + 0.25 = 0.75$. With NMS they are TP, FP, TP and $\mathrm{AP} = 0.5 + 0.5 \times 0.67 \approx 0.83$ (Example 9.5).

### Grading rubric (proposal) {#projects-rubric}

| Criterion | Weight | What earns the marks |
|---|---|---|
| Model and question | 15 % | the camera, scene and noise assumptions stated, and the question tied to a statement of the chapters (Theorem 5.2, Theorem 6.3, Proposition 10.4) |
| Correct implementation | 25 % | code written from the definitions and checked against a reference (OpenCV, COLMAP, torchvision, PyMaxflow) with a stated tolerance |
| Experimental protocol | 20 % | held-out images or sequences, several seeds or initializations, honest baselines, no tuning on the test set |
| Analysis tied to the course | 25 % | each result, failures included, explained by the course: aperture problem, local minima of ICP or k-means, disocclusion, scale of the error $Z^2\Delta d/(fB)$ |
| Communication | 15 % | figures that show the images and the errors, a talk on time, honest limits |
